stem: Authentication logs show a single failed sign-in against each of 340 different accounts over two hours, from one source. No accounts locked out. What is happening?

options.text: Password spraying
options.why: One common password tried against many accounts, deliberately staying under the lockout threshold. Wide and shallow is the signature.

options.text: Brute force
options.why: Brute force concentrates many attempts on one account, which produces a large failure count and a lockout.

options.text: Credential stuffing
options.why: Stuffing uses leaked username and password pairs and typically produces a mix of successes and failures.

options.text: A denial of service attempt against the directory
options.why: 340 attempts over two hours is negligible load. The pattern is reconnaissance for valid credentials.

stem: Why does an account lockout policy fail to stop password spraying?

options.text: The attack deliberately stays below the lockout threshold on every account
options.why: Spraying exists precisely to evade lockout. One or two attempts per account never reaches the limit, so MFA and impossible travel detection are the real answers.

options.text: Lockout policies only apply to administrative accounts
options.why: Lockout applies to whatever accounts it is configured for, typically all of them.

options.text: Spraying uses valid credentials, so nothing fails
options.why: That describes credential stuffing with known-good pairs. Spraying is guessing, and most attempts fail.

options.text: Lockout counters reset only at midnight
options.why: Reset windows vary and are not the reason. The attack simply never reaches the threshold.

stem: Within 40 minutes, 60 hosts across three subnets show the same new autostart service. No user opened an attachment and no user was logged in on most of them. What is this?

options.text: A worm
options.why: Self propagation across the network with no user action and no host file is the definition of a worm.

options.text: A virus
options.why: A virus requires a host file and a user to run it. Neither is present, and the spread rate rules it out.

options.text: A trojan
options.why: A trojan relies on a user installing something they believe is legitimate. Nobody installed anything here.

options.text: A logic bomb
options.why: A logic bomb waits for a trigger condition on a system it is already on. It does not propagate.

stem: Which characteristic distinguishes a virus from a worm?

options.text: A virus needs a host file and user action; a worm propagates on its own
options.why: This single distinction is what the exam tests, and it drives the response: a worm requires network containment first.

options.text: A virus targets Windows while a worm targets Linux
options.why: Neither is platform specific. The distinction is propagation, not operating system.

options.text: A virus encrypts data while a worm exfiltrates it
options.why: Those are payload behaviours. Either type can carry either payload.

options.text: A virus hides from antivirus while a worm does not
options.why: Hiding from detection describes a rootkit, which is a separate category.

stem: An endpoint behaves abnormally, but every tool run on the machine reports it as clean. After a full antivirus removal and reboot, the behaviour returns. What is most likely present?

options.text: A rootkit
options.why: A rootkit subverts the system below the tools, so tools running on that host cannot be trusted to report truthfully. Persistence through removal is the signature.

options.text: A trojan
options.why: A trojan describes how the malware arrived, disguised as something wanted. It does not explain why the tools see nothing.

options.text: A keylogger
options.why: A keylogger names the payload, capturing keystrokes. It does not account for the concealment.

options.text: Bloatware
options.why: Bloatware is unwanted preinstalled software. It is a nuisance, not a concealed compromise.

stem: Two weeks after a systems administrator was dismissed, a script ran on the payroll server and deleted records. Investigation shows it was scheduled months earlier to fire when that administrator's account no longer appeared in the HR feed. What is this?

options.text: A logic bomb
options.why: Malicious code lying dormant until a defined condition is met is a logic bomb, and the departure of the author is its classic trigger.

options.text: A backdoor
options.why: A backdoor provides ongoing unauthorised access. This code did not grant access, it waited and then destroyed data.

options.text: A rootkit
options.why: Nothing indicates concealment of the system's true state. The script was scheduled in the open.

options.text: Ransomware
options.why: There is no encryption and no demand. The goal was destruction, not extortion.

stem: A new laptop fleet arrives with vendor trial software, a hardware utility and a browser toolbar, all preinstalled by the manufacturer. None exfiltrates data. What is this, and why does it matter?

options.text: Bloatware: not malicious, but third-party software running with privilege that nobody in the organisation is patching
options.why: The security problem is attack surface, not surveillance. Removing it is part of establishing a secure baseline on a new build.

options.text: Spyware, because the organisation did not choose to install it
options.why: Spyware surveils and exfiltrates. The stem explicitly rules that out.

options.text: A trojan, since it arrived disguised inside a legitimate product
options.why: A trojan hides malicious function inside something wanted. Vendor bloatware is openly what it is, merely unwelcome.

options.text: Not a security concern, since it is vendor supplied
options.why: Vendor origin does not patch it. Unmaintained privileged software is exactly the surface baselines exist to reduce.

stem: Staff credentials for several unrelated services are found for sale. Investigation shows a utility installed months ago has been recording keystrokes and sending them to an external host. Which classification fits best?

options.text: Spyware, specifically a keylogger, likely delivered by a trojan
options.why: Covert surveillance with exfiltration is spyware; capturing keystrokes names the variety; arriving inside something that looked useful names the delivery.

options.text: Bloatware, since it was an unwanted utility
options.why: Bloatware is unwanted and not hostile. Data leaving the organisation settles this.

options.text: A worm, because it spread to several services
options.why: Nothing propagated. One host captured credentials used across several services.

options.text: A rootkit, because it persisted for months
options.why: A rootkit hides itself and other components, typically at or below the OS. Persistence alone does not make one.

stem: Access logs show one employee's badge opening a door at head office while the employee is confirmed on site at a different location. No forced entry is evident. What is the likely attack?

options.text: RFID cloning: the badge was read at close range and reproduced
options.why: A credential used in two places at once, with no physical damage, is the signature. Proximity reading takes seconds in a lift or a queue.

options.text: Physical brute force
options.why: That leaves damage, and the stem says there is none. The door opened legitimately as far as the reader was concerned.

options.text: Impossible travel
options.why: Impossible travel describes authentication from geographically incompatible locations. The concept is analogous and the mechanism here is a duplicated physical credential.

options.text: An environmental attack
options.why: Those target power, cooling or suppression, not access credentials.

stem: An attacker with building access disables the cooling units serving a server room. Within an hour equipment begins shutting down on thermal protection. How is this classified?

options.text: An environmental attack, producing resource inaccessibility without touching the network
options.why: Environmental attacks target the conditions equipment needs rather than the equipment. The effect is a denial of service achieved entirely physically.

options.text: A distributed denial of service
options.why: DDoS exhausts a resource using traffic from many sources. No traffic is involved.

options.text: Physical brute force
options.why: That means forcing a physical barrier such as a door or cabinet.

options.text: Resource consumption
options.why: Consumption means exhausting capacity such as bandwidth or connections. Here capacity is fine and the room is too hot.

stem: An application copies user-supplied input into a fixed-size buffer without checking length, allowing adjacent memory to be overwritten and execution redirected. Which attack is this, and what prevents it?

options.text: A buffer overflow, prevented by bounds checking in code and mitigated by protections such as ASLR and non-executable memory
options.why: The root cause is the missing length check. Platform mitigations raise the difficulty substantially and do not remove the defect.

options.text: SQL injection, prevented by parameterised queries
options.why: Injection attacks place attacker data into an interpreted statement. This one overruns memory.

options.text: A race condition, prevented by locking
options.why: Race conditions turn on timing between check and use. Nothing here is about timing.

options.text: Privilege escalation, prevented by least privilege
options.why: Escalation may be the outcome. The mechanism described is the overflow.

stem: Which indicator best distinguishes resource consumption from resource inaccessibility?

options.text: Consumption shows capacity exhausted, such as a saturated link or filled storage; inaccessibility shows a healthy resource that users simply cannot reach
options.why: One is a capacity symptom you can measure, the other is a reachability symptom. A service running comfortably that nobody can connect to points at routing, access control or a deliberate block.

options.text: Consumption is always deliberate; inaccessibility is always accidental
options.why: Either can be deliberate or accidental. The distinction is the symptom, not the intent.

options.text: Consumption affects networks and inaccessibility affects storage
options.why: Both can affect any resource type.

options.text: They are the same indicator described at different layers
options.why: The objectives list them separately because they point at different causes.

stem: Which TWO statements are correct? (Choose two.)

options.text: An environmental attack can deny service without any network traffic at all
options.why: Disabling cooling or power takes equipment down by attacking the conditions it needs.

options.text: Bloatware is not malicious but still enlarges the attack surface
options.why: Unchosen, unpatched, privileged third-party software is a real exposure even with no hostile intent.

options.text: RFID cloning requires extended physical possession of the badge
options.why: Proximity for a few seconds is enough, which is what makes it practical in a lift or a queue.

options.text: Spyware and bloatware are two names for unwanted software
options.why: One surveils and exfiltrates; the other is merely unwelcome.

options.text: Physical brute force and environmental attacks both leave visible damage
options.why: An environmental attack may leave nothing but a tripped breaker or a disabled cooling unit.

stem: Which TWO log patterns most strongly suggest a credential has been compromised rather than a user mistyping? (Choose two.)

options.text: Two successful logins from cities 9,000 km apart, 20 minutes apart
options.why: Impossible travel. Both succeeded, so this is not a typing problem.

options.text: The same account active in two sessions simultaneously from different networks
options.why: Concurrent session usage. One person cannot be in two places.

options.text: Twelve failed logins on one account followed by a lockout
options.why: That is brute force or a stale saved password. Nothing succeeded, so no credential is proven compromised.

options.text: One failed login against each of 300 accounts
options.why: That is password spraying, an attack in progress rather than evidence a specific credential is already compromised.

options.text: A password reset requested by the user through the help desk
options.why: A routine event. On its own it indicates nothing.

stem: Which TWO characteristics identify malware as a worm rather than a virus? (Choose two.)

options.text: It propagates across the network without any user action
options.why: Self-propagation with no user involvement is the defining worm behaviour.

options.text: It is a standalone program that needs no host file
options.why: A virus attaches to a host file. A worm does not need one.

options.text: It encrypts files and demands payment
options.why: That is a payload. Either type can carry it, so it does not classify the malware.

options.text: It hides itself from security tools
options.why: Concealment describes a rootkit, which is a separate category.

options.text: It arrives disguised as useful software the user installs
options.why: That is a trojan, and it requires exactly the user action a worm does not need.

stem: An attacker sends 60 byte DNS queries with a spoofed source address to open resolvers, which return 3,000 byte responses to the victim. Which term best describes the multiplication effect?

options.text: Amplification
options.why: A small request producing a much larger response multiplies the attacker's bandwidth, which is the definition of amplification.

options.text: Reflection
options.why: Reflection is also present, since the resolvers bounce traffic to the spoofed victim. The question asks specifically about the size multiplier.

options.text: An on-path attack
options.why: The attacker is not positioned between two communicating parties reading or altering traffic.

options.text: A replay attack
options.why: Nothing captured earlier is being resent. These are freshly generated queries.

stem: A victim's logs show flood traffic arriving from thousands of legitimate, well known NTP servers that the victim never contacted. What does this indicate?

options.text: A reflected attack using a spoofed source address
options.why: The attacker sent requests to those servers while forging the victim's address, so the innocent servers' replies land on the victim and conceal the true origin.

options.text: Those NTP servers have been compromised and are now part of a botnet
options.why: Reflection needs no compromise. The servers are simply answering what looks like a legitimate request.

options.text: An on-path attacker is intercepting the victim's time synchronisation
options.why: Nothing is being intercepted or modified. The victim is receiving unsolicited flood traffic.

options.text: The victim's own NTP client is misconfigured
options.why: The victim never sent these requests, which is the whole point of source address spoofing.

stem: An attacker captures an authentication message and submits it unchanged 40 minutes later. The server accepts it. Which control would have prevented this?

options.text: Including a nonce or timestamp so each message is valid only once
options.why: Replay is defeated by making every authentication message unique and time bound, so a recording cannot be reused.

options.text: Increasing the password complexity requirement
options.why: The attacker never needed the password. They reused the authentication message itself.

options.text: Certificate pinning on the client
options.why: Pinning defends against on-path interception with a fraudulent certificate. It does not stop a captured message being replayed.

options.text: Rate limiting failed logins
options.why: The replayed attempt succeeds on the first try, so it never triggers a failure threshold.

stem: An attacker positions themselves between a user and a banking site, presenting a fraudulent certificate, and alters the destination account number in a transfer request in real time. What is this?

options.text: An on-path attack
options.why: The attacker sits between the parties and modifies traffic live, which is what distinguishes on-path from a replay.

options.text: A replay attack
options.why: Replay resends a previously captured message unchanged. Here the message is being altered as it passes.

options.text: Cross site request forgery
options.why: CSRF tricks the victim's own browser into issuing a request. It does not require an interception position.

options.text: A downgrade attack
options.why: A downgrade forces weaker cryptography during negotiation. Here a fraudulent certificate is used, not a weakened cipher.

stem: An account authenticates successfully from Dublin at 09:02 and from Kuala Lumpur at 09:26. Which indicator is this?

options.text: Impossible travel
options.why: Two successful logins separated by more distance than could be covered in the elapsed time. It suggests the credential is in more than one person's hands.

options.text: Account lockout
options.why: Lockout follows repeated failures. Both of these attempts succeeded.

options.text: Out-of-cycle logging
options.why: That describes activity at an unusual time of day for the account, not an impossible geographic jump.

options.text: Missing logs
options.why: Both events are present in the log. Nothing is missing.

stem: While investigating a suspected compromise, an analyst finds the security event log has no entries between 02:10 and 02:55, though the system was running. How should this be treated?

options.text: As an indicator of compromise, since something likely cleared or suppressed the log
options.why: Missing logs are evidence in themselves. Clearing logs is a standard anti-forensic step, and it is exactly why logs are forwarded off host.

options.text: As a benign gap, since nothing happened during that period
options.why: A running system generates events. A silent window during a suspected compromise is the opposite of reassuring.

options.text: As out-of-cycle logging
options.why: Out-of-cycle logging means events appearing at unusual times, not events being absent.

options.text: As a false positive from the SIEM
options.why: The SIEM has not raised an incorrect alarm. The source data itself has a hole in it.

stem: An attacker interferes with a TLS handshake so the client and server agree on an obsolete protocol version with known weaknesses. What is this?

options.text: A downgrade attack
options.why: The negotiation is manipulated so both parties settle on weaker cryptography. The fix is to stop offering the weak versions at all.

options.text: A collision attack
options.why: A collision means two different inputs producing the same hash. No hash function is being attacked here.

options.text: A birthday attack
options.why: The birthday attack is the probability technique that makes finding hash collisions cheaper. It is not about protocol negotiation.

options.text: A replay attack
options.why: Nothing captured earlier is being resent. The live handshake is being manipulated.

stem: A researcher produces two different PDF documents that share an identical MD5 digest. What does this demonstrate?

options.text: A hash collision, showing MD5 is unfit for integrity or signature use
options.why: Two distinct inputs producing the same digest breaks the guarantee that a matching hash means identical content.

options.text: A downgrade attack against the hashing algorithm
options.why: Downgrade attacks manipulate protocol negotiation. Nothing is being negotiated here.

options.text: That MD5 encryption has been broken
options.why: MD5 is a hash function, not encryption. It has no key and nothing to decrypt.

options.text: A birthday attack, which is a different thing from a collision
options.why: The birthday attack is the technique used to find collisions efficiently. The result demonstrated here is the collision itself.

stem: A web server log shows requests containing ../../../../etc/passwd in a filename parameter. Which attack is this?

options.text: Directory traversal
options.why: Relative path sequences used to escape the intended directory and read files elsewhere on the file system.

options.text: SQL injection
options.why: No SQL is present and nothing is being passed to a database. The payload is a file path.

options.text: Privilege escalation
options.why: Reading the file may support escalation later. The mechanism in the log is path traversal.

options.text: Cross site scripting
options.why: XSS executes script in a victim's browser. This payload targets the server's file system.

stem: A logged-in user visits a malicious page, which silently causes their browser to submit a password change request to their banking site using their existing session. What is this?

options.text: Cross site request forgery
options.why: The victim's own authenticated browser is tricked into issuing a request they never intended, and the bank sees it as legitimate.

options.text: Cross site scripting
options.why: XSS executes attacker script within the vulnerable site's own origin. Here no script runs on the bank's site; the browser is simply made to send a request.

options.text: An on-path attack
options.why: The attacker never intercepts traffic. They rely entirely on the victim's browser and existing session.

options.text: Privilege escalation
options.why: No additional rights are obtained. The attacker uses exactly the rights the victim already has.

stem: Users report being disconnected from the wireless network repeatedly. A capture shows a flood of deauthentication frames claiming to come from the access point, after which several clients associate to an access point advertising the same SSID from outside the building. Which two changes address this most directly?

options.text: Set Protected Management Frames to required and deploy wireless intrusion detection for duplicate SSIDs
options.why: PMF authenticates management frames, which stops forged deauthentication. Wireless IDS detects the impersonating access point, which is an evil twin.

options.text: Increase transmit power and rotate the passphrase
options.why: Signal strength is a race the attacker can win, and a passphrase change does nothing about unauthenticated management frames.

options.text: Disable SSID broadcast so the attacker cannot clone the name
options.why: Clients transmit the SSID in probe requests, so a hidden name is easy to learn and easy to clone.

options.text: Enable MAC filtering on the legitimate access point
options.why: The attack takes place on the attacker's access point, which will not enforce your filter list.

stem: A wireless sweep discovers an access point inside the building broadcasting the corporate SSID, not managed by IT, with a stronger signal than the nearest legitimate access point. How is this best classified?

options.text: An evil twin
options.why: It impersonates the legitimate SSID in order to attract client associations, which is what distinguishes an evil twin from a merely unauthorised access point.

options.text: A rogue access point only
options.why: It is a rogue access point, but the cloned SSID makes it specifically an evil twin, and the exam wants the more precise term.

options.text: A misconfigured mesh extender
options.why: Nothing in the scenario suggests a sanctioned device. It is unmanaged and impersonating the corporate name.

options.text: A jamming device
options.why: Jamming denies service with interference. This device is offering service in order to capture clients.

stem: An employee plugs a personal wireless router into a spare office network port so they can use their tablet. The router broadcasts its own SSID, not the corporate one. How should this be classified and what control prevents it?

options.text: A rogue access point, prevented by 802.1X port security or network access control on the wired ports
options.why: It is unauthorised but does not impersonate the corporate SSID, so it is a rogue access point rather than an evil twin. Authenticating the wired port stops an unknown device joining at all.

options.text: An evil twin, prevented by wireless intrusion detection
options.why: It advertises its own name, not a clone of the corporate SSID, so it does not meet the definition of an evil twin.

options.text: An on-path attack, prevented by enabling PMF
options.why: Nothing indicates the employee is intercepting traffic, and PMF protects wireless management frames rather than wired ports.

options.text: Shadow IT with no available technical control, addressed by policy alone
options.why: It is shadow IT, but there is a strong technical control: authenticate the wired port so an unknown device cannot connect.

stem: An attacker sends requests to thousands of open memcached servers with the victim's address forged as the source. Each 15 byte request produces a reply tens of thousands of times larger, all of which lands on the victim. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: It is both: reflected, because forged sources send the replies to the victim, and amplified, because each reply dwarfs its request
options.why: Reflection is about who appears to send the traffic, amplification is about how much comes back. This attack uses both, which is the common large-scale pattern.

options.text: It is reflection only; amplification requires the attacker to control a botnet
options.why: Amplification needs only a protocol whose reply is much larger than its request. No botnet is involved in that multiplication.

options.text: It is amplification only; reflection requires the memcached servers to be compromised
options.why: The servers are innocent and answering normally. Forging the source address is what reflects their replies onto the victim.

options.text: It is an on-path attack, because the traffic passes through third-party servers
options.why: Nothing is intercepted or relayed between two parties. The third parties generate new traffic aimed at the victim.
